SENTINEL-X

👽
SENTINEL-X / PERSONAL LAB

Signals from my corner of the network.

My home security lab: Suricata, a Python/Flask dashboard, and the next step into Wazuh.

All projects

Where the lab stands

From test alerts to investigating them

I can now sign in to the dashboard, investigate an alert, filter by severity, review the analytics and export alerts as CSV. SQLite keeps the alert records. Suricata is still running on my Raspberry Pi 5, with the Python/Flask dashboard reading its EVE JSON events.

One exported alert was SURICATA STREAM excessive retransmissions. Seeing a rule name is the start of an investigation; it does not by itself prove an attack.

Suricata + dashboard: workingWazuh setup: in progress

What I set up

I’m using a Raspberry Pi 5 and my Windows 11 laptop. Suricata runs on the Pi. I connect over SSH, and a Python/Flask app reads the event log and displays it in my browser.

The dashboard is working, including login protection, alert investigation, severity filtering, analytics, CSV export and SQLite storage. I’m continuing to test it as I add the next part of the lab.

I ran a Linux command in the wrong terminal

I tried to open the dashboard file with nano while I was still in Windows PowerShell. PowerShell returned “nano is not recognized.” I needed to connect to the Pi first, then edit the file there.

nano ~/sentinel-x-dashboard/app.py

That was a useful reminder to check the prompt before running a command. My Windows terminal and the shell on the Pi are different environments.

See the PowerShell error

Getting the app and browser connected

The Flask app runs on 127.0.0.1:5000 on the Pi. Opening localhost on my laptop does not reach that app by itself. I use an SSH tunnel from the laptop to forward the port.

I also checked whether anything was listening on port 5000 before starting the app:

sudo ss -lntp | grep ':5000'

ss lists sockets. The options show listening TCP ports and their processes; grep narrows the output to port 5000. I then started the app with the Python interpreter in its virtual environment.

~/sentinel-x-dashboard/venv/bin/python ~/sentinel-x-dashboard/app.py
See Flask running on the Pi

Checking that an alert really came through

I sent four pings to my router and checked Suricata’s alert log. The rule name was SENTINEL-X ICMP Test Alert. I then checked the same alert in the dashboard.

ping -c 4 192.168.1.1
sudo tail -n 10 /var/log/suricata/fast.log

-c 4 stops after four ping requests. tail -n 10 shows the last ten log lines. This was test traffic on my own network, not an attack.

The dashboard code I’m working on

The app reads /var/log/suricata/eve.json, separates alerts from flow events, and counts them. The table shows the time, source, destination and rule name. I added severity totals and started moving the browser updates to /api/events.

The browser fetches that endpoint before updating the counters:

const response = await fetch("/api/events");
See the code in the editor

Building the Wazuh side

I’m setting up Wazuh now. I installed Oracle VirtualBox on my Windows 11 Alienware laptop and started an Ubuntu Server VM named SENTINEL-X-WAZUH. The installer detected a 60 GB virtual disk.

The latest step I documented was Ubuntu’s guided storage setup. This phase is still in progress. I have not yet verified a running Wazuh manager, enrolled agents or alerts arriving in Wazuh.

Next I want to finish the server setup, check the Wazuh services and follow a test event through the system. I’ll add the results after I have checked them.

RONNY DONKOR / STILL BECOMING
